title: Buck and the Preacher and scoring the Louis Armstrong TV film
summary: He scored Buck and the Preacher (1972) and the 1975 Armstrong television film produced by Dick Berg.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: And then in 1975, you did -- you had the major responsibility, I think, for a big TV production based on the life of Louis Armstrong.

Yes. But prior to that though, we did the picture, 'Buck and the Preacher', which I think was 1972, which starred Sidney Poitier and Harry Belafonte, which was a picture that I did all of the music for, you know, the original music to.
And then in 1975, came the Louis Armstrong '31, which had to do with ...
Right. Who was the producer of that?
The producer of that was Dick Berg.
Right. He was somebody that you had worked with on TV before.
Oh yes. I'd done a great number of the Chrysler Theatre productions at Universal with him.
What years were those?
I think ... oh, starting maybe around '64, through Gee wiz, I don't know.
The Louis Armstrong production was filmed, or was aired I think, early this year -- early '76.
January 25th, and then it was shown just about a couple months ago.
Uh huh. But the work, of course, was done in 1975.
The work was done in 1975. I think we completed it about in October 1975.
Did you do all of the music? You did the background scoring ... ths music.

I did all of the writing that was done and the background scoring and the arrangements of the numbers that were, you know, identified with Louis Armstrong. Like "Wrap your Troubles and Dreams" and "Sleepy Time Down South" ...
And "When The Saints ..."
"When The Saints Come Marching In".
Wasn't that one?
We made sort of sketch arrangements of all of that.
Was that your first arrangement of 'When the Saints Go Marching In'?
It might have been. I don't know how I've escaped it so long!
Yes. Well, what were they trying to achieve in that Louis film?

Oh, there was a story of a year in Louis's life during which he was kind of hassled by the mob in Chicago and he was pretty glad to get out of there and make the trip to Europe, where they were really demanding appearances by Louis Armstrong, and that was his first trip to Europe. Actually, the picture ends with his taking off from New York harbor, and the rest, of course, is history.
